title: The model behind HTTP: 15 ms p50, 21 ms p95
prescribes: Load the artifact once at startup, validate the request schema before scoring, expose a health endpoint, batch where the caller allows it, and verify that the served predictions match the offline ones.
applied: Started uvicorn on port 8077 in a separate process, sent 60 real test-split customers through /predict and /predict/batch, checked four malformed-request cases, and reconciled the served scores against the offline artifact.
narrative: The service came up in 2.9s and reported model SHA 8de6a81f38b2 over /health -- the endpoint exists so a load balancer can tell 'process running' from 'model loaded', which are not the same failure.

Per-request latency is 14.5 ms median and 21.0 ms at p95 over HTTP. The same 60 customers scored as one batch take 19 ms total, 0.3 ms per customer -- 52x cheaper, because almost all of the single-request cost is HTTP and DataFrame construction rather than the model.

The reconciliation check is the one that catches deployment bugs: the served probabilities differ from the offline artifact by at most 4.82e-07 -- which is the six-decimal rounding in the JSON response, not a scoring difference. A non-trivial difference here would mean the service is not running the model that was evaluated -- the single most common way a good model becomes a bad deployment.

Schema validation is enforced by Pydantic with `extra='forbid'`, so a missing field returns 422, an unexpected field 422, a wrong type 422 and a negative charge 422. None of them are scored. Silently coercing a bad request is worse than rejecting it, because the caller gets a number back and believes it.

ONNX export: not exported -- NotImplementedError: The converter is implemented when the missing values are string not <class 'float'>.. The joblib pipeline is what ships; ONNX would be the next step for a latency-sensitive deployment.
